data.text:
Coupling of functional connectivity and regional
cerebral blood flow reveals a physiological basis
for network hubs of the human brain

Xia Liang, Qihong Zou, Yong He, and Yihong Yang

PNAS | January 29, 2013 | vol. 110 | no. 5 | 1929–1934
www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.1214900110

Forty-eight healthy adults (27.4 ± 7.1 y old, 25 females) participated in the study.
All participants were screened to ensure they had no history of neurological/psychiatric conditions or drug abuse.
Informed consent was obtained from all subjects in accordance with the guidelines and approval of the Institutional Review Board of the Intramural Research Program of the National Institute on Drug Abuse.

Scanning was performed on a 3 Tesla MR Scanner (Siemens).
All participants first underwent a resting-state BOLD and a resting-state ASL scan.
In addition, 39 of the participants also underwent a BOLD and an ASL scan while performing an N-back working-memory task.
Experiment design and MR parameters are detailed in SI Materials and Methods.

Both BOLD and ASL images were preprocessed using the Analysis of Functional Neuroimaging (AFNI) software package.
After preprocessing, these functional images were subject to the following analysis.

BOLD data were used to identify functional hubs of human brain networks by computing the functional connectivity strength (FCS) at a voxel level, i.e., the average functional connectivity between a given voxel and all other voxels in the brain.
The relationship between regional brain network properties (including functional connectivity strength, nodal efficiency, and betweenness) and rCBF during resting and task states was investigated.
The results showed high correlations of rCBF with CMRGlu (r = 0.54, P < 0.0001) and CMRO2 (r = 0.31, P = 0.005) across Brodmann areas, indicating that rCBF is tightly coupled with resting oxygen and glucose metabolism, and thus an adequate surrogate for metabolism to be used in the following analyses.

As expected, we found that the behavioral performance positively correlated with working-memory task-related changes in FCS in the right inferior-parietal lobule, and task-related changes in rCBF in the left inferior-parietal lobule at the 3-back level.

A repeated-measures analysis of variable (ANOVA) with task load (0-back, 1-back, 2-back, and 3-back) as the fixed effect revealed that rCBF/FCS ratio was significantly modulated by task load in several task-positive regions, including the left inferior- and superior-parietal lobe (IPL/SPL) and middle frontal cortex (MFC), and several task-negative regions, including the PCC/PCu and mPFC/ACC.

This article contains supporting information online at www.pnas.org/lookup/suppl/doi:10.1073/pnas.1214900110/-/DCSupplemental.
